questions.question_text: What is stored in result? double result = 7 / 2;
questions.explanation: 7 / 2 is integer division = 3, THEN assigned to a double becomes 3.0. The division happens with ints before the conversion, so the decimal is already lost.

questions.question_text: Which is a Java boolean literal?
questions.explanation: Java booleans are only true or false (lowercase keywords). Unlike some languages, integers and strings are not valid boolean values.

questions.question_text: What does Math.abs(-7) return?
questions.explanation: Math.abs returns the absolute value: |-7| = 7. It strips the sign, returning the magnitude.

questions.question_text: Given String s = "hello";, what does s.substring(5) return?
questions.explanation: substring(5) on a 5-char string starts at index 5 (just past the last char), returning the empty string "". substring(6) would throw an exception—5 is the valid boundary.

questions.question_text: What prints? int x=15; if(x%3==0 && x%5==0) System.out.print("FizzBuzz"); else if(x%3==0) System.out.print("Fizz");
questions.explanation: 15 is divisible by both 3 and 5, so the first condition is true and prints 'FizzBuzz'. The else-if is skipped once the first branch runs.

questions.question_text: The expression !true evaluates to:
questions.explanation: The NOT operator (!) negates a boolean: !true = false. It flips true to false and vice versa.

questions.question_text: How many times does the body run? int i=10; while(i>0){ i=i-2; }
questions.explanation: i goes 10→8→6→4→2→0; the body runs 5 times (subtracting 2 each iteration) until i is 0 and the condition i>0 fails.

questions.question_text: What is printed? int count=0; for(int i=1;i<=5;i++) for(int j=1;j<=5;j++) if(i==j) count++; System.out.println(count);
questions.explanation: i==j only on the diagonal (1,1),(2,2),...,(5,5) = 5 times out of 25 total iterations. The condition limits the count to matching pairs.

questions.question_text: If a class field is declared 'private int x;', it can be accessed from outside the class only through:
questions.option_d: it cannot be accessed at all
questions.explanation: Private fields are hidden from outside code; public getters/setters provide controlled access (encapsulation). Direct external access (obj.x) won't compile for private fields.

questions.question_text: The 'main' method signature in Java is:
questions.explanation: The JVM requires exactly public static void main(String[] args) as the program entry point. It's static (no object needed) and takes command-line arguments.

questions.question_text: What does this print? int[] a={2,4,6,8}; System.out.println(a[a.length-1]);
questions.explanation: a.length-1 = 3, the last valid index, holding 8. Using length-1 is the safe way to access the final element.

questions.question_text: What does this compute? int[] a={5,2,8,1}; int m=a[0]; for(int v:a) if(v<m) m=v; System.out.println(m);
questions.explanation: This finds the minimum: starting at a[0]=5, it updates m whenever a smaller value appears, ending at 1. Initializing m to a[0] handles all-value sets correctly.

questions.question_text: What is list after: ArrayList<Integer> list=new ArrayList<>(); list.add(1); list.add(2); list.set(0, 9);
questions.explanation: set(0, 9) replaces the element at index 0 with 9, giving [9, 2]. set overwrites without changing the list size, unlike add which inserts.

questions.question_text: ArrayList differs from a regular array in that an ArrayList:
questions.explanation: ArrayLists resize automatically as elements are added/removed; arrays have a fixed length set at creation. ArrayLists use methods (get/set/add), arrays use brackets.

questions.question_text: How do you find the number of rows in int[][] grid?
questions.explanation: grid.length gives the number of rows (the outer array's length); grid[0].length gives columns in the first row. Rows = outer length, columns = inner length.

questions.question_text: What does this sum? int[][] m={{1,1},{1,1},{1,1}}; int s=0; for(int r=0;r<m.length;r++) for(int c=0;c<m[r].length;c++) s+=m[r][c];
questions.explanation: A 3×2 grid of all 1s sums to 6 (3 rows × 2 columns × 1). The nested loops visit every element, adding each to s.

questions.question_text: If a subclass does not override a method, calling it on a subclass object:
questions.explanation: Subclasses inherit non-overridden methods, so the superclass implementation runs. Overriding only replaces specific methods the subclass chooses to redefine.

questions.question_text: Which is true about a subclass object assigned to a superclass reference (Animal a = new Dog())?
questions.option_a: you can call any Dog-specific method directly through a
questions.option_b: you can only call methods defined in Animal, but overridden versions run Dog's code
questions.explanation: The reference type (Animal) limits which methods you may call; the object type (Dog) determines which override executes. Dog-only methods need a cast to ((Dog)a).

questions.question_text: What does this print? void f(int n){ if(n<=0) return; System.out.print(n+" "); f(n-1);} f(3)
questions.explanation: The print happens BEFORE the recursive call, so it prints on the way down: 3 2 1. Putting print after the call would reverse the order to 1 2 3.

questions.question_text: What does this return? int f(int n){ if(n==0) return 1; if(n==1) return 1; return f(n-1)*n;}  f(4)
questions.explanation: This is factorial: f(4) = f(3)*4 = f(2)*3*4 = f(1)*2*3*4 = 1*2*3*4 = 24. Both base cases return 1 and the multiplications build the product.

questions.question_text: Which operator performs integer division remainder?
questions.explanation: The modulus operator % gives the remainder of division (7%3 = 1). The / operator gives the quotient. % is essential for checking divisibility and cycling values.

questions.question_text: What does "Java".compareTo("Java") return?
questions.explanation: compareTo returns 0 for equal strings, a negative number if the first is lexicographically before the second, and positive if after. Equal strings yield 0.

questions.question_text: A 'for-each' (enhanced for) loop is best used when you need to:
questions.option_b: read each element of a collection without needing the index
questions.explanation: The enhanced for loop cleanly iterates over each element for reading. When you need indices (to modify or skip), a standard indexed for loop is required.

questions.question_text: Two constructors in the same class with different parameter lists is an example of:
questions.explanation: Multiple constructors distinguished by parameters is overloading, letting objects be created in different ways. Overriding involves replacing an inherited method, a different concept.

questions.question_text: What happens if you try to access arr[-1]?
questions.explanation: Negative indices are invalid in Java arrays and throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. (Unlike some languages, Java doesn't support negative indexing for the last element.)

questions.question_text: Why does removing elements with a forward for-each loop throw a ConcurrentModificationException?
questions.option_b: modifying a collection during for-each iteration is not allowed
questions.explanation: Structurally modifying a list while iterating with for-each breaks the iterator, throwing ConcurrentModificationException. Use an explicit Iterator's remove() or iterate by index backward.

questions.question_text: The @Override annotation in Java:
questions.option_b: signals that a method is intended to override a superclass method, helping catch errors
questions.explanation: @Override documents intent and makes the compiler verify the method actually overrides one—catching typos in the signature. It's good practice though not strictly required.

questions.question_text: The two essential parts of every recursive method are the base case and the:
questions.option_b: recursive case (which calls the method on a smaller problem)
questions.explanation: The base case stops recursion; the recursive case reduces the problem and calls the method again. Both are required—missing the base case causes infinite recursion.

questions.question_text: Given int x=5; which expression is true?
questions.explanation: x=5: x>=5 is true AND x<10 is true → true. Option A fails (x>5 is false), C fails (both false), D fails. Inclusive >= matters when x equals the boundary.
